description:
A proven English course creator sells $200K a year on Kajabi or Udemy, and roughly two-thirds of global e-learning demand sits outside North America. The tools they can buy today stop at the words. HeyGen dubs the video for $29 to $330 per month. Rask does the same for $60 to $750. Kajabi ships native dubbing in 100+ languages on its $249 and $499 plans. None of them find the Brazilian buyer, run the Portuguese ads, answer the WhatsApp question at 10pm, or handle the tax. So the creator ships an English course to an English audience and leaves the rest of the world on the table.

This idea sells the finished sale in-country, not the translation step. One stack pairs the creator with a vetted local operator (translator, marketer, support), runs one checkout, splits the money automatically, and charges only when a new international sale happens. The creator approves each market with one click, keeps 70% of revenue that did not exist before, and never hires a Brazilian marketer at 11pm.

newLayoutSections.Why Now:
YouTube shipped multi-language audio to millions of creators on Sept 10, 2025

Three things changed in the last twelve months, and all three point at the same customer. First, on September 10, 2025, YouTube rolled out multi-language audio to millions of creators after a two-year pilot with MrBeast, Mark Rober and Jamie Oliver. Pilot creators saw over 25% of their watch time come from viewers in the video's non-primary language, and Jamie Oliver's channel got a 3x view lift. Meta shipped an AI dubbing and lip-sync tool for Reels the month before. The distribution channels where course creators already live now expect a dubbed version, not an English original.

Second, the price of getting the words right collapsed. Traditional studio dubbing ran $50 to $200 per finished minute. AI dubbing in 2026 runs $1 to $10 per minute at the entry tier, and $0.55 to $2.40 per minute on creator plans. A 10-minute video that cost $500 to $2,000 to dub in a studio now costs $10 to $100. That is a 60 to 90% cut, and it happened in about 18 months.

newLayoutSections.The Verdict:
Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

Udemy instructors with thousands of students publicly ask on the official forum for translation control they cannot get, so the buyer is real, named, and gathering in one place you can DM.
The unit economics work at small scale: 10 pilots at $2,500 setup plus a 20% platform take on $18K/pilot in year-one international sales lands around $80K-$150K in year one with just one operator plus AI agents doing the drafts.
The wedge (finished sale in-country, not just translated words) is a real remainder AI does not touch: local ads, WhatsApp support, checkout, tax, and the cultural rewrite that turns a translated line into one that sells.
HeyGen at $200M ARR and Rask at 1,600 monthly branded searches prove creators already pay for the translation step, so the market is warm even if this specific offer has to be sold, not searched for.

REASONS TO NOT BUILD

Zero people per month search for 'translate online course', 'course translation service', or 'course reseller program' on Google Ads, so every customer is a cold-outbound close with no pull demand to lean on.
Every 2025-2026 tailwind (YouTube free multi-language audio, Kajabi native dubbing on Growth $249/mo, Meta AI dub for Reels) gives proven creators a reason to keep 100% and skip a partner entirely, which is the exact opposite of what a royalty-split marketplace needs.
This is a two-sided sales business dressed as a marketplace: you have to close a US creator on Monday and a Brazilian growth marketer on Friday, and marketplace liquidity needs 5-10 vetted operators per country before it works.
HeyGen (100,000 paying customers, ~$200M ARR) or Kajabi can add a 'local partner' tab to their existing distribution in six months and eat the wedge before the founder has 50 paying creators.
Roast it with your agent

POTENTIAL PIVOT

Drop the two-sided marketplace and royalty-split story. Start as a done-for-you international launch service for one country at a time, priced as a flat setup fee plus a rev share only on international sales the creator was not making. Recruit in-country operators as 1099 contractors first, not marketplace partners. Prove the finished-sale unit works with 10 creators in Brazil or Mexico before adding a second country or a partner-side product. The marketplace can come later, after supply and demand are both real.

The Full Idea.text:
A proven English course creator sells $200K a year on Kajabi or Udemy, and roughly two-thirds of global e-learning demand sits outside North America. The tools they can buy today stop at the words. HeyGen dubs the video for $29 to $330 per month. Rask does the same for $60 to $750. Kajabi ships native dubbing in 100+ languages on its $249 and $499 plans. None of them find the Brazilian buyer, run the Portuguese ads, answer the WhatsApp question at 10pm, or handle the tax. So the creator ships an English course to an English audience and leaves the rest of the world on the table.

This idea sells the finished sale in-country, not the translation step. One stack pairs the creator with a vetted local operator (translator, marketer, support), runs one checkout, splits the money automatically, and charges only when a new international sale happens. The creator approves each market with one click, keeps 70% of revenue that did not exist before, and never hires a Brazilian marketer at 11pm.

A founder starts by picking one country and one language, not five. Brazil and Mexico are the sharpest first shots: Latin America e-learning was $30.51B in 2024 and grows at 9.3% a year, with Brazil holding 25%+ of the region. The founder recruits three in-country operators as 1099 contractors before recruiting the first creator, and vets them on a $200 paid trial (one 5-minute dubbed sample plus one landing-page rewrite). Then the founder does outbound to named instructors on Udemy, Kajabi Hero and Teachable, offering a free International Revenue Audit: a one-page memo showing the top three countries by demand from the creator's own YouTube and Kajabi geo data, projected earnings, and a named local operator ready to run each one.

The genuinely hard part is not the software. AI agents draft the audits, run the outbound and write the workflow code. The hard part is closing both sides of the trade. On one side, a proven US creator has to trust a stranger with 20% of their international revenue. On the other, a Brazilian growth marketer has to take a share deal instead of a $4,000/mo agency retainer. That is a two-sided sales business dressed as a marketplace, and it needs a founder who has already sold something to course creators (ran a course, worked at Kajabi or Teachable, ran a creator agency) and is comfortable running trust-based deals in two languages.

The wedge customer is the Udemy or Kajabi instructor with 5,000 to 100,000 students on one English course who already sees non-English demand in their analytics and has publicly asked for a way to translate. Udemy's own community forum has multi-year threads where instructors with tens of thousands of students beg the platform for translation control they cannot get, and independent creators on X call the current AI dubbing stack 'almost scammy' at $50/mo. These are named, gathered people you can DM this week.

The money is a free lead magnet, a $2,500 setup fee for the first market (60 days, one country) at a 30% rev share for 12 months, then a standing 20% platform take on each additional country the creator approves. A vetted operator pool pays $99/mo for private deal flow. Ten pilots plus their first year of international sales land around $80K to $150K in year one. Ceiling depends on operator supply and creator retention, not tech: with 40 active creators averaging three countries each, the honest ceiling is $2M to $4M ARR before an incumbent (HeyGen, Kajabi) is likely to add a 'local partner' tab and force this business to either specialize by vertical or move upmarket to publishers.

The Full Timing Case.text:

TIMING

AI dubbing collapsed to $1-10/min and Kajabi shipped native translation in Sept 2025, which makes the market ready for localization but also lets creators skip a partner entirely.

Three things changed in the last twelve months, and all three point at the same customer. First, on September 10, 2025, YouTube rolled out multi-language audio to millions of creators after a two-year pilot with MrBeast, Mark Rober and Jamie Oliver. Pilot creators saw over 25% of their watch time come from viewers in the video's non-primary language, and Jamie Oliver's channel got a 3x view lift. Meta shipped an AI dubbing and lip-sync tool for Reels the month before. The distribution channels where course creators already live now expect a dubbed version, not an English original.

Second, the price of getting the words right collapsed. Traditional studio dubbing ran $50 to $200 per finished minute. AI dubbing in 2026 runs $1 to $10 per minute at the entry tier, and $0.55 to $2.40 per minute on creator plans. A 10-minute video that cost $500 to $2,000 to dub in a studio now costs $10 to $100. That is a 60 to 90% cut, and it happened in about 18 months.

Third, the course platforms stopped watching from the sidelines. Kajabi announced its largest ever product upgrade on September 16, 2025 and shipped native AI transcription, translation and dubbing in 100+ languages across Courses, Websites and Landing Pages by December 29, 2025. Translation is now a native Kajabi workflow, not a plug-in.

The non-English demand is where the money is going. Latin America e-learning was $30.51B in 2024 and is projected at $52.1B by 2030, a 9.3% CAGR. Asia-Pacific e-learning is growing at roughly 20.9% a year. North America is about 35% of the global e-learning market, so roughly two-thirds of the world's course spend sits in non-English regions, and it is compounding faster than the English base.

THE SIGNALS

Honest counter: every one of these tailwinds also makes pure DIY translation more attractive. Cheaper AI dubbing, native Kajabi dubbing and free YouTube multi-language audio all let a solo creator ship a Spanish or Portuguese version without splitting a dollar with a partner. The timing case is strong for translating a course; it is weaker for licensing a course.
The real "now" for a partner network is the leftover work that AI does not touch: in-country checkout and tax, local ads and creator relationships, WhatsApp-first support, and the cultural rewrite that turns a translated line into one that sells. That work has not gotten cheaper.
What would make "now" wrong: if YouTube's free auto-dub plus Kajabi's built-in translation are already "good enough" for the top 20% of creators to pocket 100% and skip a partner entirely. If that happens, this business exists only for the long tail that cannot self-serve, and the deal sizes shrink.

The Opening (Full Market Analysis).text:
The competitive map for turning an English course into money in a new country has five camps, and every camp stops before the sale.

The AI dubbing tools own the mind-share. HeyGen is the giant: 175+ languages, over 100,000 paying business customers, roughly $200M ARR. Rask AI is the runner-up: 130+ languages, voice cloning in 32, sold at $60 to $750 per month by dubbed-minute credits. Both sell the same job: turn English video into translated video. Neither sells the customer, the checkout, the support ticket, or the local marketing that decides if the course actually earns money in-country.

The course hosts bolt on a translation feature and stop. Kajabi ships native transcripts, translations and dubbing (Wistia under the hood, 70+ languages) on its Growth ($249/mo) and Pro ($499/mo) plans, metered by AI credits, and the creator still has to duplicate the product per language by hand. Thinkific has no native translation at all; the official answer is duplicate the course and translate the copy yourself, or on the Plus plan run a second Thinkific site for each language. Weglot is the popular add-on that translates the storefront and funnel pages into 110+ languages, but it does not touch video and does not localize checkout or split payouts.

The enterprise localization agencies handle the full stack but sell to L&D departments. SimulTrans, Stepes, Pangea, IKHYA and DTP Labs quote a 60-minute course per language at low four figures to five figures: per-word translation at $0.10 to $0.30, voice-over at multiple dollars per finished minute, plus engineering. The buyer is a corporate learning team on a project budget, not a solo creator on a rev share.

Udemy is the closest thing to the pitched model and it is a warning, not a template. Udemy hosts 9,200+ native-language courses and does auto-translate captions, but it keeps 63% of marketplace sales and picks which courses get translated with no way for the instructor to request it. The two loudest complaints in the instructor forum (Phillip Burton at 79,000 students, the tech instructor asking for a subtitle tool) are exactly the pain a partner marketplace would solve, if the take rate stayed well under 63% and the creator picked the markets.

The PLR (Private Label Rights) market is the DIY status quo for reselling someone else's course: courses sold on Janets and Gumroad starting at $10 to $200 with rebrand rights and no royalties back to the original author. This is the anti-model: one-time sale, no quality control, no creator upside. It exists because there is real demand to resell courses in new markets, and it is served badly.

The honest gap: no named player packages the four pieces (translation + dubbing + in-country marketing + one-checkout royalty split) into a single deal a creator can approve with a click. That gap is real. What is unproven is whether creators will pay a partner 20% to fill it, or whether YouTube's free multi-language audio and Kajabi's built-in dubbing make them try DIY first.

Your way in: One stack that bundles translation plus a vetted local partner plus checkout plus royalty math. Rask does words only.

THE IDEA

A proven English course creator sells $200K a year on Kajabi or Udemy, and roughly two-thirds of global e-learning demand sits outside North America. The tools they can buy today stop at the words. HeyGen dubs the video for $29 to $330 per month. Rask does the same for $60 to $750. Kajabi ships native dubbing in 100+ languages on its $249 and $499 plans. None of them find the Brazilian buyer, run the Portuguese ads, answer the WhatsApp question at 10pm, or handle the tax. So the creator ships an English course to an English audience and leaves the rest of the world on the table.

This idea sells the finished sale in-country, not the translation step. One stack pairs the creator with a vetted local operator (translator, marketer, support), runs one checkout, splits the money automatically, and charges only when a new international sale happens. The creator approves each market with one click, keeps 70% of revenue that did not exist before, and never hires a Brazilian marketer at 11pm.

WHY NOW

YouTube shipped multi-language audio to millions of creators on Sept 10, 2025

Three things changed in the last twelve months, and all three point at the same customer. First, on September 10, 2025, YouTube rolled out multi-language audio to millions of creators after a two-year pilot with MrBeast, Mark Rober and Jamie Oliver. Pilot creators saw over 25% of their watch time come from viewers in the video's non-primary language, and Jamie Oliver's channel got a 3x view lift. Meta shipped an AI dubbing and lip-sync tool for Reels the month before. The distribution channels where course creators already live now expect a dubbed version, not an English original.

Second, the price of getting the words right collapsed. Traditional studio dubbing ran $50 to $200 per finished minute. AI dubbing in 2026 runs $1 to $10 per minute at the entry tier, and $0.55 to $2.40 per minute on creator plans. A 10-minute video that cost $500 to $2,000 to dub in a studio now costs $10 to $100. That is a 60 to 90% cut, and it happened in about 18 months.

THE VERDICT

Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

Udemy instructors with thousands of students publicly ask on the official forum for translation control they cannot get, so the buyer is real, named, and gathering in one place you can DM.
The unit economics work at small scale: 10 pilots at $2,500 setup plus a 20% platform take on $18K/pilot in year-one international sales lands around $80K-$150K in year one with just one operator plus AI agents doing the drafts.
The wedge (finished sale in-country, not just translated words) is a real remainder AI does not touch: local ads, WhatsApp support, checkout, tax, and the cultural rewrite that turns a translated line into one that sells.
HeyGen at $200M ARR and Rask at 1,600 monthly branded searches prove creators already pay for the translation step, so the market is warm even if this specific offer has to be sold, not searched for.

REASONS TO NOT BUILD

Zero people per month search for 'translate online course', 'course translation service', or 'course reseller program' on Google Ads, so every customer is a cold-outbound close with no pull demand to lean on.
Every 2025-2026 tailwind (YouTube free multi-language audio, Kajabi native dubbing on Growth $249/mo, Meta AI dub for Reels) gives proven creators a reason to keep 100% and skip a partner entirely, which is the exact opposite of what a royalty-split marketplace needs.
This is a two-sided sales business dressed as a marketplace: you have to close a US creator on Monday and a Brazilian growth marketer on Friday, and marketplace liquidity needs 5-10 vetted operators per country before it works.
HeyGen (100,000 paying customers, ~$200M ARR) or Kajabi can add a 'local partner' tab to their existing distribution in six months and eat the wedge before the founder has 50 paying creators.

POTENTIAL PIVOT

Drop the two-sided marketplace and royalty-split story. Start as a done-for-you international launch service for one country at a time, priced as a flat setup fee plus a rev share only on international sales the creator was not making. Recruit in-country operators as 1099 contractors first, not marketplace partners. Prove the finished-sale unit works with 10 creators in Brazil or Mexico before adding a second country or a partner-side product. The marketplace can come later, after supply and demand are both real.

The founder who wins this is not a translator and not a coder. It is an operator who has already sold something to online course creators (previously ran a course, worked at Kajabi/Teachable/Podia, ran a creator agency, or built a large creator email list), and who is comfortable doing hard two-sided sales: closing a $2,500 pilot with a US creator on Monday, then closing a Brazilian marketer on Friday to run that pilot. AI agents can draft the audits, run the outbound, and write the workflow code. What agents cannot do is convince a proven creator to trust a stranger with 20% of their international revenue, and convince a Brazilian growth marketer to take a share deal instead of an agency retainer. This is a sales and trust business dressed in a marketplace, and it needs a founder who has real credibility on both sides.
